passage: Mahima, you run a team now, so here's the thing I wish someone had told me. When I became lead at the app studio, every developer gave me dates like "Thursday, easy." And every Thursday slid to the next Tuesday. My first instinct was: they're lazy, or they don't care. But I'm Deepak, I was a developer for years, and I did exactly the same thing. It isn't laziness. It's how people picture work: the smooth version, no bugs, no meetings. So I changed two things. I ask for a range now: best case, likely case, worst case. And every month we put last month's estimates next to what really happened. No blame, just numbers. Our dates are still hopeful. But they're hopeful with their eyes open.

qa.a: Deepak asks for a range: best case, likely case, worst case.

qa.q: Why did Deepak stop thinking the developers were lazy?
qa.a: Remembering doing exactly the same thing as a developer, Deepak saw the rosy dates as how people picture work, not as not caring.

qa.q: Why does the monthly comparison help, on top of the ranges?
qa.a: Putting last month's estimates next to what really happened, without blame, lets everyone learn how far off they usually are.

qa.q: How might the developers feel about the new approach?
qa.a: They'd likely feel less judged, since slipping dates are treated as a shared habit to fix, not proof of laziness.

grounding: A team lead explains seeing repeated optimistic dates as ordinary human thinking, then asking for ranges and reviewing past accuracy.

Zeenat, you've just become a lead, and you're annoyed that everyone's dates slip. Sit down; let me, Tanuja, tell you about my first year leading the data team in 2012.
Every Monday, my analysts promised, "Friday, ma'am." Every Friday, it became Wednesday next week. I thought they were careless. Then one weekend I went through six months of our tracker, date promised versus date delivered. Nearly every task was late, by roughly the same margin. The most hardworking people were the most hopeful.
That changed how I saw it. They weren't lazy; everyone, me included, imagined the smooth version.
So I stopped asking, "When will it be done?" and started asking, "What's the earliest, and what's the latest if things go wrong?" Every month we looked back together: how close were our ranges? Nobody felt blamed. After a year, our deliveries were on time far more often.

qa.a: She compared date promised versus date delivered.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja stop thinking her analysts were careless?
qa.a: Tanuja felt surprised to see nearly every task late by a similar margin, even among the hardest workers, which convinced her it was a common habit of imagining the smooth version, not laziness.

qa.q: What two changes did Tanuja make, and how did they help?
qa.a: She asked for an earliest and latest date instead of one date, and reviewed the ranges each month without blame, so deliveries became more reliable.

qa.q: How might the analysts have felt once Tanuja began asking for ranges?
qa.a: They likely felt less judged and more honest about uncertainty, since nobody was blamed and they could say what might go wrong.
